text: The king was shaken. He went up to the chamber over the gate and wept, and as he went he cried out, "My son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! If only I had died instead of you—Absalom, my son, my son!"
Joab was told, "Look, the king is weeping and mourning for Absalom."
So the victory that day was turned into mourning for all the troops, because that day they heard it said, "The king is grieving over his son."
The troops slipped into the city that day like men who steal away in shame after fleeing from battle.
The king had covered his face, and he cried out at the top of his voice, "My son Absalom! Absalom, my son, my son!"

Then Joab came to the king in the house and said, "Today you have shamed all your servants, who this very day saved your life, and the lives of your sons and daughters, your wives and your concubines.

You love those who hate you and hate those who love you. Today you have made it plain that your commanders and your servants mean nothing to you. I see clearly that if Absalom were alive and all of us dead today, that would suit you well.

Now get up, go out, and speak kindly to your servants. For I swear by the LORD, if you do not go out, not a single man will stay with you tonight, and that will be worse for you than every disaster that has come upon you from your youth until now."

So the king got up and took his seat in the gateway, and word was passed to all the troops: "The king is sitting in the gate." Then all the troops came before the king. Meanwhile Israel had fled, every man to his tent.

Throughout all the tribes of Israel the people were arguing with one another: "The king rescued us from the hand of our enemies; he delivered us from the hand of the Philistines. But now he has fled the land because of Absalom,
and Absalom, whom we anointed over us, has died in battle. So why do you say nothing about bringing the king back?"

King David sent word to Zadok and Abiathar the priests: "Speak to the elders of Judah and say, 'Why should you be the last to bring the king back to his house, when the talk of all Israel has already reached the king where he is staying?
You are my brothers; you are my own bone and flesh. Why then should you be the last to bring the king back?'
And say to Amasa, 'Are you not my own bone and flesh? So may God do to me, and more also, if you do not become commander of my army for all time, in place of Joab.'"

versions.text: And say to Amasa, 'Are you not my own bone and flesh? So may God do to me, and more also, if you do not become commander of my army for good, in place of Joab.'"
versions.explanation: "For good" is ambiguous when read aloud (it can be heard as "for a good purpose"). Hebrew כל־הימים means "all the days / permanently"; "for all time" renders it clearly and keeps the rhythm.

text: So he won over the hearts of all the men of Judah as though they were one man, and they sent word to the king: "Come back, you and all your servants."
So the king set out on his return and came to the Jordan, and Judah came to Gilgal to meet the king and bring him across the Jordan.
Shimei son of Gera, the Benjaminite from Bahurim, hurried down with the men of Judah to meet King David.
With him were a thousand men from Benjamin, and Ziba, the steward of Saul's household, with his fifteen sons and twenty servants. They rushed down to the Jordan ahead of the king
and crossed at the ford to bring the king's household over and to do whatever he thought best. Shimei son of Gera threw himself down before the king as he was about to cross the Jordan
and said to him, "Let my lord not hold me guilty. Do not remember the wrong your servant did on the day my lord the king left Jerusalem; may the king not take it to heart.
For your servant knows that I have sinned. But see, today I have come, the first of all the house of Joseph, to come down and meet my lord the king."
Then Abishai son of Zeruiah spoke up: "Should Shimei not be put to death for this? He cursed the LORD's anointed!"

But David said, "What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah, that you should turn against me today? Shall a single man be put to death in Israel today? Do I not know that today I am king over Israel?"
So the king said to Shimei, "You shall not die," and the king gave him his oath.

Mephibosheth son of Saul also came down to meet the king. He had not cared for his feet or trimmed his mustache or washed his clothes from the day the king left until the day the king came home safely.

versions.text: Mephibosheth son of Saul also came down to meet the king. He had not cared for his feet or trimmed his mustache or washed his clothes from the day the king left until the day he came back in peace.
versions.explanation: The pronoun "he" is ambiguous for a listener, since the sentence begins with Mephibosheth as its subject; the Hebrew refers to the king's safe return. Naming the king removes the ambiguity in oral reading.

text: When he came to meet the king in Jerusalem, the king asked him, "Why did you not go with me, Mephibosheth?"
He answered, "My lord the king, my servant deceived me. Your servant said, 'I will saddle my donkey and ride it and go with the king'—for your servant is lame.
But he slandered your servant to my lord the king. Still, my lord the king is like an angel of God; do whatever seems good to you.

My father's whole house deserved nothing but death from my lord the king, yet you set your servant among those who eat at your table. What further claim do I have, and what right to appeal to the king?"
The king said to him, "Why go on talking? I have said it: you and Ziba shall divide the land."
And Mephibosheth said to the king, "Let him take it all, now that my lord the king has come home in peace."
Barzillai the Gileadite came down from Rogelim and crossed the Jordan with the king, to escort him across the river.

versions.text: Barzillai the Gileadite came down from Rogelim and went with the king to the Jordan to see him on his way across.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew says Barzillai actually crossed the Jordan with the king (וַיַּעֲבֹר... הַיַּרְדֵּן), not merely that he accompanied him as far as the river. Verse 40 then shows Barzillai turning back after the crossing.

versions.text: Barzillai the Gileadite came down from Rogelim and crossed the Jordan with the king, to send him on his way.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew infinitive לְשַׁלְּחוֹ אֶת־הַיַּרְדֵּן specifies the escorting as being 'over the Jordan'; 'to send him on his way' loses the sense of accompanying him across. 'To escort him across the river' keeps the object without repeating 'Jordan' awkwardly and reads smoothly aloud. The current rendering is a defensible general translation of שַׁלַּח.

text: Barzillai was very old, eighty years of age. He had provided the king with food during his stay at Mahanaim, for he was a very wealthy man.
The king said to Barzillai, "Cross over with me, and I will provide for you at my side in Jerusalem."
But Barzillai answered the king, "How many years of life are left to me, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem?

I am eighty years old today. Can I still tell good from bad? Can your servant taste what he eats or drinks? Can I still hear the voices of men and women singing? Why should your servant be one more burden to my lord the king?
Your servant will only cross the Jordan with the king a little way. Why should the king reward me like this?

Please let your servant turn back, so that I may die in my own town, near the grave of my father and mother. But here is your servant Kimham; let him cross over with my lord the king, and do for him whatever seems good to you."
The king said, "Kimham shall cross over with me, and I will do for him whatever seems good to you; and anything you ask of me I will do for you."
So all the people crossed the Jordan, and the king crossed too. Then the king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and Barzillai returned home.
The king went on to Gilgal, and Kimham went with him. All the men of Judah escorted the king across, and half the men of Israel as well.

Then all the men of Israel came to the king and said to him, "Why did our brothers, the men of Judah, steal you away and bring the king and his household across the Jordan, along with all the men of David?"

versions.text: Then all the men of Israel came to the king and said to him, "Why did our brothers, the men of Judah, steal you away and bring the king and his household across the Jordan, along with all David's men?"
versions.explanation: For oral reading, "all the men of David" flows better than the possessive "all David's men" at the end of a long sentence; the abrupt shift from "you" to "the king" reflects the Hebrew and may be kept, but a footnote noting the shift in person would help hearers.

text: The men of Judah answered the men of Israel, "Because the king is our close relative. Why does this make you angry? Have we eaten anything at the king's expense? Has he given us any gift?"

versions.text: The men of Judah answered the men of Israel, "Because the king is our close relative. Why does this make you angry? Have we eaten anything at the king's expense? Have we taken anything for ourselves?"
versions.explanation: The second clause (נִשֵּׂאת נִשָּׂא לָנוּ) describes something being carried or presented to them, i.e. a gift received from the king, rather than something they seized; the parallel with the first question is about benefits from the king, not self-serving action.

text: The men of Israel answered the men of Judah, "We have ten shares in the king, so we have a greater claim on David than you do. Why then did you treat us with contempt? Were we not the first to speak of bringing back our king?" But the men of Judah spoke even more fiercely than the men of Israel.
